set.typical_award_size: 855 East Laurel Drive (County-owned, declared exempt surplus August 31, 2022; Eden Housing selected with the City of Salinas through an RFQ September 2022; ENA February 17, 2023): 132-unit 100% affordable rental project (53 low, 48 very low, 29 extremely low income, 2 manager units) in two phases (78 and 54 units) approved by the Board on February 28, 2025 with a Lease Disposition and Development Agreement and a 99-year Ground Lease at $1.00 per year; groundbreaking targeted for late 2026 subject to local funding then tax credits. The adjoining SHARE Center (845 East Laurel Drive, 128-bed navigation center) is being reconfigured with twelve non-congregate family cabins and a 30-bed recuperative care area using a Central California Alliance for Health Housing Fund award of $3,222,262 and Health Department match for a $6,444,524 budget (October 30, 2026, Resolution 26-194).
set.layering_notes: Monterey County's Housing and Community Development Department (HCD, Craig Spencer, Director; Darby Marshall, Housing Program Manager) runs the Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, the Monterey County Housing Trust Fund, PLHA, the Urban County CDBG and HOME programs and County land dispositions; the County Administrative Office Homelessness Strategies and Initiatives Division (CAO-HSI) runs HHAP and the SHARE Center; the Health Department Behavioral Health Bureau holds BHSA; the Coalition of Homeless Services Providers leads the CoC (CA-506, shared with San Benito); and the Housing Authority of the County of Monterey (HACM) and its Development Corporation supply vouchers and develop housing. Salinas, Monterey, Seaside and other entitlement cities run their own programs (Pass 3). countyofmonterey.gov blocks automated access (pages and documents), so records were built from the Legistar web API client 'monterey' and its Granicus attachments, hamonterey.org, chsp.org, zoneomics and HCD tables. East Laurel Drive is the model for County participation: land by ground lease plus trust fund and PLHA loans, with the City of Salinas as co-sponsor; the Alliance Housing Fund award shows Medi-Cal plan capital is available for interim and recuperative housing in the county. Source is the February 28, 2025 Board approval item (Legistar file RES 25-041); SHARE Center details from file RES 26-194. Funding type set to land: the County's contribution is a 99-year ground lease of about five acres at $1.00 per year under the LDDA (Attachment A, Detailed Discussion, RES 25-041).

reason: Board item confirms the County contribution is a 99-year ground lease at $1.00 per year, so funding_type is land rather than other.

set.typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. The City Code (Section 8-1.00 et seq., Ordinance 3346 C.S. of 2004 requiring permanent affordability) requires a minimum of 20% permanently affordable low and moderate income units in projects of six or more new housing units and in condominium conversions (2015-2023 Housing Element Program i.2.1), with payment of in-lieu fees allowed; the 2015-2023 Housing Element reported that court rulings had limited the ordinance to ownership projects and that it did not apply to apartment projects; the 2023-2031 Housing Element Program 2-I directs the City to codify the requirement in the Zoning Code. The City holds a first right to repurchase deed-restricted ownership units and resells them to low income buyers using CDBG program income ($729,609 generated from such sales in 2025). Portfolio: 531 restricted units (100 inclusionary ownership, 431 deed-restricted rental) plus 42 in development; 2300 Garden Road delivered 13 inclusionary units in a 91-unit project in 2025.
set.audit_note: Audit 2026-11-08: redirect was to files.monterey.gov (same PDF). The FY 2026-27 Action Plan confirms the 531-unit portfolio (100 ownership, 431 rental, 42 in development), $729,609 program income from inclusionary unit sales, the first right to purchase, Program 2-I and 2300 Garden Road. It does not state the 20% rule; the City's 2015-2023 Housing Element does, with a six-unit threshold and an ownership-only limit at that time. Whether the City now applies the ordinance to rental projects (post AB 1505) was not confirmed; the code host monterey.municipal.codes returns 403.

reason: Applicability threshold was missing: the ordinance applies to projects of six or more units and condo conversions, and the City's Housing Element reported it applied only to ownership projects.

set.typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan (draft, City CDBG page): about $275,000 CDBG entitlement plus $256,750 program income and $49,250 prior year funds, $581,000 total, allocated by Council on March 19, 2026. The FY 2026-28 NOFA anticipated $525,000 (FY 2026-27) and $500,000 (FY 2027-28) and caps planning and administration at 20% and public services at 15%, with the remaining 65% for public facilities and infrastructure; public service grants are guided to $5,000 to $12,000. New housing construction is ineligible except by Community Based Development Organizations, and FY 2026-27 awards went to public services and facility projects (including the Elm House transitional housing roof). The fifth cycle Housing Element (HCD review draft, March 2020) reported an Inclusionary Housing In-Lieu Fund of about $2.6 million as of 2017, historically granted to nonprofit developers to buy existing housing or build new affordable units; no current balance was found. Successor Agency Long Range Property Management Plan sites were identified for residential and mixed use sale.

set.next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The next two-year CDBG NOFA (FY 2028-30) is expected in late 2027 if the City repeats the prior cycle timing; in-lieu fund awards are ad hoc.

set.layering_notes: Seaside controls three small local layers (CDBG entitlement, in-lieu fund, successor agency land) but CDBG is used for public services and public facilities, not new housing construction, so it is not a gap source for multifamily development. A developer should approach Community Development about the in-lieu fund or sites such as Campus Town (about 297 planned affordable units), the North 40, Parker Flats and 1620 Broadway; the Action Plan also cites the Seaside Housing Collaborative for acquisition and rehabilitation. County HHAP, County Housing Trust Fund and HACM project-based vouchers (county records) are the larger sources. CDBG figures come from the City's CDBG page, the draft FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan and the FY 2026-28 NOFA; the in-lieu fund figure is from the 2020 Housing Element draft hosted by HCD.

set.typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Ordinance 2025-07 (introduced May 20, 2025, adopted June 3, 2025, effective 30 days later, implementing Housing Element Program 2.4 with General Plan Amendment Resolution 2025-48) lowered the threshold from 20 to 5 or more units and set a citywide 20% requirement for new or substantially rehabilitated for-sale or rental housing: 6% very low, 7% low, 7% moderate, plus a voluntary incentive-based 10% middle income (up to 135% AMI for-sale) tier; existing occupied housing on the former Fort Ord also 20% (6/7/7), down from 40% (15/15/10). Market-rate density bonus units are exempt. Alternatives approved by Council (17.48.030(D)): land dedication, acquisition and rehabilitation, preservation of at-risk units, conversion of market-rate units, special needs housing, or a tailored program for 500-unit specific plan projects. No in-lieu fee is codified; the Affordable Housing Trust Fund (17.48.090) receives only enforcement recoveries. Rental units restricted 55 years (in perpetuity if allowed), for-sale resale restrictions 45 years, rents capped at 90% of comparable market rent.
set.next_deadline: Applies with the first discretionary application (affordable housing plan required). Housing Element objective: 200 lower income units through inclusionary and density bonus by 2031.
